extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists writing technical documents (students, researchers, authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for writing clear, correct, and well-organized mathematical and CS technical documents (papers, proofs, theses, programs, manuals), with emphasis on exposition, notation, typesetting, and editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate adjacent symbols with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols in different formulas must be separated by words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: Consider Sq, q < p.  Good: Consider Sq, where q < p. Put words between adjacent formulas so the prose reads smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t start sentences with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning a sentence with a bare mathematical symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: xn − a has n distinct zeroes. Good: The polynomial xn − a has n distinct zeroes. This prevents parsing problems and improves flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using logical symbols in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t use symbols like ., ⇒, ∀, ∃, ∃ in running text; replace them with the corresponding words (except in logic works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write out words for clarity in most expositions; use formal symbols only where conventional and expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preceding statement to theorem must be a complete sentence or end with a colon
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement just preceding a theorem, algorithm, etc., should be a complete sentence or should end with a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'We now have the following' (then Theorem.). Good: 'We can now prove the following result.' Theorem. The function H(x) defined in (5) is continuous. Prefer also to give suggestive motivation tying the theorem to prior discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make theorem statements self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of a theorem should usually be self-contained, not depending on assumptions only in preceding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary restate assumptions within the theorem or refer to the exact definitions; avoid implicit dependencies on earlier sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' to avoid passive voice; avoid 'I' unless relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'we' to create a conversational author–reader partnership; avoid 'I' in formal technical writing unless the author's persona matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'We' should mean 'you and me together'; when multiple authors use 'we' the ambiguity is acceptable or can be resolved with parenthetical clarifications (e.g., 'one of the authors (DEK)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit for sentence rhythm and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a definite rhythm in sentences; read what you have written and change wording if it does not flow smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose phrasing that matches cadence; sometimes only one of several synonyms will have the correct rhythm. Use hearing (reading aloud) to check flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep 'that' when it helps parsing; avoid gratuitous 'that'
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t omit 'that' when it helps the reader parse the sentence, but avoid 'that' used as padding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: Assume A is a group. Good: Assume that A is a group. But avoid 'We have that x = y' — say 'We have x = y.' Use judgment based on cadence and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure; use parallelism where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary sentences to avoid monotony but use parallelism when parallel concepts are being discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetitive sentence openers; ensure parallel constructs are syntactically parallel (example contrasting textbook/laboratory phrasing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t write homework-style sequences of formulas; add running commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid listing a sequence of formulas with no connecting prose; tie concepts together with exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the purpose of each displayed or inline formula and how it connects to surrounding ideas; provide signposts for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: State definitions/ideas twice, complementarily
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to state things twice in complementary ways (especially definitions) to reinforce understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give both formal definition and an intuitive description or example; define all variables (at least informally) where first introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate the reader and keep reader knowledge in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Always ask: What does the reader know so far? What should the reader expect next and why? Motivate results and definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing others’ work, prefer letting the results speak or give reasons why they are interesting; when describing your own work, be humble and avoid superlatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write so sentences survive formula-skimming
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers will skim formulas on first reading; sentences should still flow when formulas are replaced by a placeholder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sentences remain grammatical and meaningful even when complex formulas are mentally glossed over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent notation and avoid reusing symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t use the same notation for two different things; use consistent notation for the same thing in different places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow typographic conventions (lowercase for elements, uppercase for sets) and choose index names consistently (e.g., i from 1..m, j from 1..n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize and manage subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t get carried away by subscripts, especially nested subscripts; avoid naming elements when not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer referring to unspecified elements x,y of X rather than x1,...,xn if indices are not needed; use element notation to avoid subscript proliferation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important formulas and number only important ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Display crucial formulas on their own line and number only the important display equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a displayed formula will be referenced later, number it; avoid numbering every display unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure left-to-right readability and avoid ambiguous sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should be readable from left to right without ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'Smith remarked in a paper about the scarcity of data.' or 'In the theory of rings, groups and other algebraic structures are treated.' Reorder to make subject–verb relations clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out small numbers when used as adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Small numbers should be spelled out when used as adjectives, but not when used as names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example distinctions: 'Method 2' vs 'requires 17 passes' vs 'increased by 2' — choose form that matches syntactic role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize formal names (Theorem, Lemma, Algorithm, Method) in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize terms like Theorem 1, Lemma 2, Algorithm 3, Method 4 in headings/captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent capitalization aids readability and indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch common grammatical pitfalls (maxims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of common pitfalls: sentence-final prepositions, dangling participles, fragments, pronoun–antecedent agreement, unnecessary commas, splitting infinitives — apply judgment rather than slavish rule-following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are heuristics to watch for; sometimes breaking a rule is best for clarity or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary or obscure jargon and overly dense notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist the temptation to use jargon or unnecessarily complex symbolic presentations when clearer, more accessible wording exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer readable, familiar vocabulary when possible; long or dense symbolic statements can be replaced by clearer prose or standard named theorems for accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humor and jokes sparingly and appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is best used when readers understand the joke only by understanding a technical point; avoid jokes that will not survive re-reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict to in-jokes that reinforce a technical idea and that the intended audience will appreciate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and be consistent about tense and narrative sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Either use present tense throughout or write sequentially (past/present/future markers) — consistency aids comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential writing suits long papers; use temporal words to signal chronology when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical notation, not programming notation, in papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish mathematical notation from programming notation; prefer subscripts over programmatic indexing and use juxtaposition for multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in formal papers use p_r instead of p[r]; prefer xy to x * y. Use notation expected by the mathematical audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate roles (element vs component) with language
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose terminology to distinguish relationships: call pr a 'component' of p rather than an 'element' to avoid confusion between set membership and vector components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about the type of relationship you mean; consistent vocabulary reduces reader errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put words between adjacent formulas and manage ellipses spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember to insert words between adjacent formulas; when using ellipses, place commas before/after as required and get dot-level and spacing right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use commas around '(P1, . . . , Pn)'; ensure ellipses alignment depends on surrounding punctuation and operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid linebreaks inside formulas and use typesetting controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Linebreaks in the middle of formulas are undesirable; enforce no-breaks with typesetting tools (TeX commands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
TeX and other systems provide mechanisms (
obreak, ties) to prevent awkward line breaks; check math breaks in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t overuse colons; capitalize after a colon only for full sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive colon use; if the text after a colon is a full sentence, capitalize the first word, otherwise do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Define it as follows:' is fine; but 'We have: formula' should usually omit the colon since the formula completes the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extraneous parentheses and nested parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many parentheses, especially nested ones, hurt readability; remove unnecessary outer parentheses when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer '(Definition 2)' to '(definition (2))' unless the latter is unavoidable due to display numbering; typographers may use larger outer parentheses for nested pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sparing with fonts, capitalization, and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t overuse typographic effects (many fonts, ALL CAPS, excessive boldface)—they distract the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic conventions judiciously and consistently; rely on standard emphasis techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark end of proofs clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a box or 'Q.E.D.' to mark the end of a proof; if using a box, leave a space between it and the final period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear end-of-proof markers help readers scan and locate proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make paragraph breaks clear around displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure it is clear where new paragraphs begin and end, especially when displayed formulas are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spacing, indentation, or short signpost sentences to indicate paragraph boundaries near displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use notational/typographic conventions appropriate to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions like boldface vectors or arrows over vectors are helpful if appropriate for the intended readership; prefer roman type for ordinal suffixes (i+1st) to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose conventions that signal meaning clearly and conform to audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid psychologically bad line breaks; use nonbreaking spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent awkward or misleading line breaks (e.g., leaving a final symbol alone) by using nonbreaking spaces or ties in typesetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In TeX, use a tilde (~) to tie words/symbols; check final layout to avoid line-break artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spelling checkers and watch for frequent misspellings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use spelling tools and be aware of commonly misspelled words (list provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common misspellings (impliment/implement, dependant/dependent, etc.) should be corrected; maintain clean orthography for professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply 'name and conquer' to long expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overly long formulas by naming frequently used subexpressions so manipulation is clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: replace v = c + u(ci − cj + 1) with v = c + ku, where k = ci − cj + 1 when that subexpression is reused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize unnecessary subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer minimal subscript usage; don't index elements unless needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'pi ∈ P' can often be written 'p ∈ P' to reduce clutter and cognitive load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before or very near their first use
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce and define notation at first appearance (at least informally) to avoid reader confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a symbol can't be defined immediately, provide an informal description or locate the definition close by.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotony of sentence openers but maintain parallelism when intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t use the same sentence-starter repeatedly; however, use parallel structure intentionally when making parallel points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary phrasing for readability; reserve repetitive structure only to emphasize parallel points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise: choose words that match logical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use vocabulary that precisely matches the intended logical meaning (e.g., 'not nonincreasing' ≠ 'increasing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sloppy antonyms or vague qualifiers; prefer unambiguous formulations even if slightly longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed tenses on the same subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistent tense usage for a given subject to prevent awkwardness and reader confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either write in present tense or use sequential narrative where past/present/future are signposted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proofs over proofs by contradiction when it improves exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use proof by contradiction if a direct proof is available and clearer for exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct proofs often avoid unnecessary assumptions and may generalize better; use contradiction for problem-solving but prefer direct style for final presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide signposts and conversational tone to guide readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational tone with explicit signposts, transition paragraphs, and short commentary helps readers follow complex arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phrases like 'The operative word is zero', 'We divide the proof into two parts' to keep the reader oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep index ordering and relational phrases consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to indexed components (i < j), keep index order consistent when comparing p_i and p_j (avoid flipping i and j positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say 'p_i < p_j' and keep i/j in the same relative positions to help the reader visualize relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite in multiple passes, prefer handwritten drafts early
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewriting improves writing; consider drafting by hand to match thinking speed and then retyping and typesetting with further passes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may perform many rewrites, sometimes discarding and starting over; use successive passes to focus on different problems (flow, clarity, typesetting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value professional editors and designers
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors and book designers add value—don’t ignore professional editorial/design help even with self-publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers decide layout, fonts, margins; copy editors catch punctuation/grammar/style errors and improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful distinguishing mathematical numerals from text numerals and font choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When using specialized math fonts (e.g., Euler), ensure mathematical numerals are distinguished typographically from text numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some faces use a slashed or dotted zero for mathematics; set mathematics and text numerals correctly during typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid changing punctuation conventions carelessly (quotes vs parentheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow standard but logical punctuation rules: commas/periods conventionally go inside quotation marks; punctuation with parentheses should be logically applied to the parenthesized sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put a period inside parentheses only if the entire sentence is within parentheses; otherwise apply punctuation to the outer sentence as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of audience conventions when hyphenating compound terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenation decisions (e.g., programming-language notation) depend on disciplinary norms; follow the audience’s expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In computer science, 'random number generator' and 'floating point arithmetic' are common without hyphens; hyphenation can look wrong to insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincident punctuation is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincident punctuation (e.g., comma next to another punctuation mark) is not inherently a sign of bad construction and should be handled by standard rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where two punctuation marks coincide, follow the conventional single-mark rule (e.g., comma + period => period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize material clearly and appreciate non-linear organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization (beyond linear order) matters: weave branches and alternative threads together to create a coherent exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on the overall plot/organization of a manuscript; good organization is recognized by readers even when hard to define.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stylistic choices that distract
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not distract the reader with stylistic quirks that do not aid communication; anything that helps communication is good, anything that hurts is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a stylistic device—notation change, screaming ungrammatical sentence, awkward repetition—is used, justify it as a deliberate device to jar or emphasize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use punctuation and word choices that minimize distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid usages that raise hackles (e.g., controversial uses of 'hopefully') or stylistic choices (excessive exclamation points) that distract readers from content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a usage is likely to distract an authoritative subset of your audience, consider avoiding it; prefer clarity and unobtrusiveness.
